title: Financial statements
intro: Accounting is the language every other chapter speaks. You do not need to be an auditor, but you must read the three statements fluently, explain why profit differs from cash, and trace any transaction through all three without hesitating. This is the most tested topic in finance interviews at every level.

title: Performance analysis
intro: Accounting tells you what happened; performance analysis tells you why, and whether it will continue. Interviewers use ratio questions to test judgement: which numbers you look at first, how you connect them, and what you conclude. The goal is not to recite forty ratios but to explain a business in five.

title: Finance mathematics
intro: Two ideas sit under all of valuation: a rupee today is worth more than a rupee tomorrow, and a risky rupee is worth less than a safe one. This chapter covers the arithmetic of time (discounting, NPV, IRR), the price of risk (cost of capital), and the tools that show how sensitive an answer is to its assumptions.

title: Valuation
intro: Valuation is where accounting, finance maths and judgement meet. Every finance interview will ask you to value something or defend a value. The methods are simple; the skill is choosing the right one, making assumptions you can defend, and presenting a range with a recommendation rather than a single false-precise number.

title: Capital structure and capital markets
intro: Companies fund themselves with a mix of debt and equity, raised privately or in public markets, and return surplus cash through dividends and buybacks. Every track needs this chapter: bankers execute these transactions, CFOs choose among them, and investors price them. Indian rules change often, so learn the logic first and check the current thresholds before an interview.

title: Markets, macro and professional tools
intro: Technical knowledge gets you through the first round. What wins later rounds is evidence that you think like someone already doing the job: you follow markets, you can connect a macro event to a company, you build clean models quickly, and you communicate a recommendation in two minutes. This chapter covers those professional habits.

title: How investment banks work
intro: An investment bank sells two things: advice on transactions and access to capital. Its clients are companies, their promoters and large shareholders, and governments. Before you learn any deal mechanics, understand how the bank is organised, who does what, how it gets paid, and which firms matter in India.

title: Mergers and acquisitions
intro: M&A work is about running a process that produces the best outcome for your client: the right buyer at the right price with the right terms and certainty of closing. Interviewers test whether you know the sequence, the documents, the economics and the Indian regulatory steps.

title: Equity capital markets
intro: ECM is the largest source of investment banking fees in India. You should be able to explain the IPO process end to end, the difference between a fresh issue and an offer for sale, how book building sets the price, and which route a listed company should use to raise money.

title: Debt capital markets and acquisition finance
intro: Debt teams help companies borrow from bond investors and lenders. The analysis is the mirror image of equity: instead of upside, lenders focus on the downside, cash flow coverage, security and covenants.

title: The work product: models, pitchbooks and deal discussions
intro: Associates spend most of their time producing three things: models, client documents and analysis of deals. Interviewers probe whether you understand the purpose of each and can do a credible version quickly.

title: What IB interviews test
intro: Campus IB processes in India run through a buddy call, two or three technical rounds with associates and VPs, and a senior round with a director or MD. Recent interview reports from Indian business schools show a consistent pattern: a stock or sector pitch is central, technical questions are standard but probed deeply, and "why IB, why this bank" is asked in every round.

title: The CFO organisation and operating cadence
intro: Corporate finance roles sit inside a company, close to the decisions. The CFO's organisation plans the year, measures what happened, explains why, keeps the books and controls honest, manages cash and risk, and decides where capital goes. To interview well, you need to know which team does what, how the annual cycle runs, and how finance earns a seat at the table.

title: FP&A: planning, forecasting and variance
intro: Financial planning and analysis turns strategy into numbers, then tells management every month whether the numbers are being delivered and why not. The best FP&A people are trusted by business leaders because they explain drivers, not accounting lines.

title: Business finance and investment decisions
intro: Business finance partners sit with a brand, sales region, plant or product line and help it make money-making decisions: what to charge, which customers and channels to serve, what to make or buy, and which projects to fund.

title: Treasury: cash, funding and risk
intro: Treasury makes sure the company never runs out of cash, borrows at the lowest sensible cost, and is not blown off course by currency or interest rate moves. The work is quantitative, market-facing and increasingly strategic.

title: Reporting, controls and Ind AS
intro: Controllership keeps the numbers right and on time. It is the foundation of investor trust, and for CAs it is the fastest route to credibility in a corporate finance interview, as long as you can connect accounting to business decisions.

title: Capital allocation and CFO-track interviews
intro: The CFO's most important job is allocating capital: deciding which projects, acquisitions and payouts get the company's cash. Interviews for CFO-track roles test whether you can think like that owner, and whether you can structure a messy business problem.

title: How private equity works
intro: A private equity firm is two businesses: it raises money from institutions, and it invests that money in companies. To interview well you need both halves: how fund economics shape behaviour, and how a deal team decides what to buy, at what price, and how it will exit.

title: Sourcing, screening and due diligence
intro: Most of a PE associate's time goes into deciding which companies deserve attention and testing whether an investment thesis survives contact with the facts. The best diligence tries to disprove the thesis, not confirm it.

title: LBO mechanics and returns
intro: The leveraged buyout model is the most tested technical skill in PE interviews, even in India where many deals are minority growth investments. It tests whether you understand where returns come from: growing earnings, paying down debt with cash flow, and buying and selling at sensible multiples.

title: Execution, the IC memo, ownership and exits
intro: Deals are won and lost in execution: the sequence of letters, approvals and documents that turn interest into a signed transaction. After closing, the fund's job becomes making the business worth more and selling it well.

title: What PE interviews test
intro: PE interviews in India are small, fast and demanding. Seats are few and usually go to candidates with banking, consulting, Big 4 deals or buy-side experience, but strong candidates from other backgrounds get through by showing investment judgement. Expect a stock or company pitch, business model questions, a paper LBO or returns question, and deep questions about the fund.

title: How venture capital works
intro: Venture capital funds back young companies whose success, if it comes, is enormous. Because most startups fail, a VC fund's returns come from a handful of outliers. That single fact explains how VCs size markets, how much ownership they want, how they build portfolios and why they say no to good businesses.

title: Evaluating startups: market, team, product and traction
intro: Early-stage investing is judgement under uncertainty. There is little financial history, so VCs evaluate the market, the team, the product insight and the earliest evidence of demand, and they look for reasons a startup could become very large, not reasons it is safe.

title: Term sheets, instruments and cap tables
intro: Valuation in venture is set by negotiation, not by a DCF, and the terms matter as much as the headline price. You must be fluent in pre-money and post-money, dilution, option pools, convertible instruments and liquidation preferences.

title: What VC interviews test
intro: VC interviews are conversations about markets and founders. The best evidence of fit is work you have already done: a market map, a memo, a thesis you have written about, startups you have met. Technical questions are lighter than in IB or PE, but cap tables and metrics must be flawless.

title: Consulting and deal advisory
intro: Many ISB students interview for consulting and finance in the same season. The two overlap more than people think: strategy firms run private equity due diligence and corporate finance projects, and Big 4 deal advisory teams do valuation, diligence and M&A work that looks a lot like banking. This chapter covers the finance-heavy corners of consulting and how their interviews differ.

title: Equity research and asset management
intro: Equity research analysts form and publish views on listed companies; asset managers invest clients' money in them. Both reward accounting skill, a defensible opinion and the discipline to say what would prove you wrong. The stock pitch is the centre of every interview.

title: Markets, trading and treasury
intro: Markets roles (sales and trading in FX, rates, credit and equities, and bank treasury) are the most macro-driven finance jobs. Interviews spend half their time on current events and your views, and the rest on derivatives and fixed income basics. Preparation cannot be crammed: follow markets daily for weeks.

title: Corporate banking, credit and project finance
intro: Corporate bankers and credit analysts decide whether and how to lend. The mindset is the opposite of equity investing: the upside is capped at interest and fees, so the job is understanding everything that could go wrong and structuring protection against it. Private credit funds, a fast-growing buy-side employer, use the same skills.
